title: ICMR Says Northern Hemisphere Flu Shot Best Matches India's Circulating Strains — Use Southern Hemisphere Only Until Supply Catches Up
summary:
Indian influenza surveillance finds circulating H1N1, H3N2 and B/Victoria viruses closely match the WHO Northern Hemisphere 2026–27 trivalent vaccine. Programme and clinical guidance is to prefer that formulation — and to use the Southern Hemisphere shot only as a bridge when Northern Hemisphere stock is short.

A July 2026 note from India's influenza surveillance system — the DHR–ICMR Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory (VRDL) network working with the WHO National Influenza Centre at ICMR–National Institute of Virology (NIV), Pune — concludes that phylogenetic analysis of circulating strains aligns with WHO's Northern Hemisphere (NH) vaccine recommendation for 2026–27. The practical line is clear: the NH vaccine is ideal; if it is not available, use the Southern Hemisphere (SH) vaccine already in the market and switch to NH as soon as supply allows.

That guidance drew sharper attention in September 2026 as H1N1-driven influenza activity rose in Delhi-NCR and elsewhere, and as clinicians and distributors reported uneven access to preferred products.

## What the surveillance network saw

India runs year-round influenza testing through 73 sentinel sites under the VRDL network, with characterisation at the National Influenza Centre at ICMR–NIV Pune, a WHO Collaborating Centre within the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS).

From 1 July 2025, the centre received or obtained 73 influenza isolates: 3 influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, 52 A(H3N2), and 18 influenza B (Victoria lineage). Forty-nine isolates underwent whole-genome sequencing. Phylogenetic analysis of the haemagglutinin gene showed circulating H1N1, H3N2 and B/Victoria viruses largely matched the WHO-recommended NH 2026–27 vaccine components.

All 73 isolates tested for antiviral susceptibility by phenotypic assay were sensitive to oseltamivir — useful for clinicians managing severe influenza while product choice is debated.

WHO issues separate NH and SH compositions each year. The July Indian note lists the NH 2026–27 egg-based trivalent recommendation as including an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus, an A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like virus, and a B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus, with closely related alternatives for cell-culture and recombinant platforms. The SH 2025 composition differs on the H3N2 and B components — which is why antigenic match, not brand habit, drives the preference for NH in the current Indian data.

## Prefer NH; bridge with SH if needed

Because surveillance shows close resemblance between circulating Indian strains and the NH recommendation, the note says it would be ideal to administer the NH vaccine; however, in view of non-availability of the NH vaccine, the available SH vaccine may be used and replaced with NH as soon as NH becomes available.

In early September 2026, coverage of H1N1 surges and pharmacy shortages amplified that bridge language. ICMR later clarified that appropriate seasonal influenza vaccines, including NH formulations, are available through leading pharmacies and may be taken voluntarily — particularly by people at higher risk of severe disease. The clarification does not erase the July match finding. It reframes the problem as distribution, demand spikes, and local stock-outs rather than a permanent absence of NH product.

For district and hospital pharmacy teams, the workable rule remains: stock and offer NH when you can get it; do not leave high-risk patients unvaccinated while waiting; document which hemisphere product was given so a later NH dose can be planned if SH was used as a stopgap and local clinical guidance supports switching when NH arrives.

## Who should be prioritised — and what India does not yet fund

India does not currently deliver annual influenza vaccination through the Universal Immunisation Programme. Uptake has historically been low. India Today reporting around the September surge put private-market prices in the range of about ₹2,000–2,500 per dose — a meaningful out-of-pocket barrier outside employer schemes and private insurance.

ICMR guidance continues to prioritise people at higher risk of severe influenza: older adults, pregnant women, people with underlying comorbidities, and immunocompromised individuals.

## Implications for public health practice

For epidemiologists and programme officers, the July note is a surveillance-to-procurement story: year-round VRDL/NIC data should drive which hemisphere product districts try to stock.

For clinicians advising high-risk patients, prefer NH 2026–27 when available. If only SH is on the shelf, vaccinate with SH rather than delay, and revisit NH when supply normalises. Oseltamivir remains a rational antiviral choice for eligible severe cases given uniform sensitivity in the characterised isolate set — recognising that 73 isolates are a laboratory series, not a national resistance survey.

For policy watchers, the deeper gap is unchanged: influenza vaccination in India is still mostly a private-pay prevention tool layered onto a UIP that does not yet carry an annual flu antigen. Match recommendations only help if product reaches the people who need it at a price they can pay.

Sources: NCDC/ICMR–NIV July 2026 influenza vaccine composition note (VRDL/NIC surveillance); India Today and ThePrint reporting on the July note and September 2026 ICMR clarification on pharmacy availability.

title: Indian Sentinel Study Finds Pneumococcal Meningitis Share Falling After PCV Rollout
summary:
Early Indian hospital surveillance after pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) introduction shows a clear drop in the share of pneumococcal meningitis among young children admitted with suspected meningitis — and a shift away from vaccine-covered serotypes.

An ICMR-supported meningitis network enrolled 12,971 children aged 1–59 months across 32 tertiary hospitals between 2019 and 2022. Pneumococcal meningitis was confirmed in 303 of those children (2.3%). When investigators divided the calendar into pre-PCV, early-PCV, and post-PCV windows around India’s real-world product switch — PCV13 in selected sites, then nationwide PCV10-SII (PNEUMOSIL) — the proportion of meningitis that was pneumococcal fell from 3.5% before introduction to 1.8% in both the early- and post-PCV periods.

That kind of aetiologic fraction is exactly what programme and surveillance teams hope to see when a new antigen enters the Universal Immunisation Programme. It does not, by itself, prove a drop in population incidence. But it is hard to ignore when it lines up with a serotype story that matches the vaccine.

## Serotype shift mirrors the vaccine

Among cases with serotyping available, serotypes included in PCV10-SII declined from 41.4% before PCV to 25.9% after broader use. Residual disease still featured non-vaccine serotypes such as 18C/18B, 8, and 10F. Those leftovers matter. Conjugate vaccines reshape the landscape; they do not erase pneumococcus. For residents reading IDSP alerts or talking to paediatric wards, the question after PCV is no longer only “is coverage high?” but “which serotypes are still landing in hospital, and are they the ones we expected?”

Where outcome data were available, case fatality among pneumococcal meningitis cases was 6.9%. That figure should be read cautiously — tertiary referral hospitals enrich for severe disease — but it keeps the clinical stakes visible.

## How the study was built

The design is sentinel and hospital-based, not a community cohort. That is both a strength and a limit. Strength: you get microbiologically characterised meningitis from a large multi-centre network over years that bracket a policy change. Limit: referral patterns, lab capacity, and clinical suspicion can move proportions even when true community risk is flat. The authors’ periodisation around the PCV13-to-PCV10-SII transition is the feature Community Medicine trainees should steal for journal club: define the intervention window clearly, then track both the bug fraction and the serotype mix.

## Why this matters on the ground

For MD Community Medicine, the paper is a workable evaluation template more than a single success headline. It shows how to:

- Periodise surveillance around a real UIP antigen change  
- Pair aetiologic endpoints with serotype endpoints  
- Interpret hospital meningitis signals in the years after introduction  
- Keep residual non-vaccine types on the watch list for AEFI rounds, district immunisation reviews, and conversations with clinicians who only see “meningitis” on the discharge summary  

Coverage charts will still dominate many district meetings. This study is a reminder to ask for the microbiology underneath them.

Source: *Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia* (open access), DOI 10.1016/j.lansea.2026.100790.
